data.reference_solution:
def removeNthFromEnd(head: Optional[ListNode], n: int) -> Optional[ListNode]:
    nodes = []
    curr = head
    while curr:
        nodes.append(curr)
        curr = curr.next
    sz = len(nodes)
    target_idx = sz - n
    if target_idx == 0:
        return head.next
    prev = nodes[target_idx - 1]
    to_remove = nodes[target_idx]
    prev.next = to_remove.next
    return head

data.key_insight: By maintaining a gap of n nodes between a fast pointer and a slow pointer, when the fast pointer reaches the end of the list, the slow pointer will be positioned right before the node that needs to be removed.

data.reference_solution:
def removeNthFromEnd(head: Optional[ListNode], n: int) -> Optional[ListNode]:
    values = []
    curr = head
    while curr:
        values.append(curr.val)
        curr = curr.next
    sz = len(values)
    target_idx = sz - n
    new_values = values[:target_idx] + values[target_idx+1:]
    dummy = ListNode(0)
    tail = dummy
    for val in new_values:
        tail.next = ListNode(val)
        tail = tail.next
    return dummy.next

data.pattern_summary: Using two pointers moving at different offsets or speeds to traverse a sequential structure in a single pass. Reach for this when you need to find a relative position from the end of a list without knowing its length ahead of time.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. We can offset one pointer by n steps so that when it hits the end, the other pointer is at the target.

pattern_options.name: Hash map lookup
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Storing nodes in a hash map uses unnecessary extra space when pointers can track relative positions.

pattern_options.name: Binary search
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. A linked list does not allow random access, so binary search cannot be applied here.

pattern_options.name: Dynamic programming
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. There are no overlapping subproblems or optimal substructure needs for this traversal task.

signals.phrase: removing the nth node from the end
signals.hint: Implies a target distance relative to the unknown end of the sequence.
Prohibits calculating the total length in a first pass before deleting in a second pass.

data.brute_force_idea: Traverse the entire linked list to collect all node values into an array, calculate the total length and the removal index, splice out the target value, and then rebuild a new linked list from the remaining values.
data.brute_force_why: We iterate through the linked list to build the array, and then iterate again to rebuild the new linked list.
data.bottleneck: The code must traverse the entire list just to find its length before it can determine where the target node is located.
bottleneck_hints: Think about what information you are missing when you first start at the head.
Can you find the target position without knowing the total length of the list first?
Consider how maintaining a fixed distance between two moving references could reveal the target position on the fly.
data.brute_force_code:
def removeNthFromEnd(head: Optional[ListNode], n: int) -> Optional[ListNode]:
    values = []
    curr = head
    while curr:
        values.append(curr.val)
        curr = curr.next
    sz = len(values)
    target_idx = sz - n
    new_values = values[:target_idx] + values[target_idx+1:]
    dummy = ListNode(0)
    tail = dummy
    for val in new_values:
        tail.next = ListNode(val)
        tail = tail.next
    return dummy.next

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The brute force approach requires two passes over the data: one to collect values and another to build a new list, plus extra memory to store those values. The optimized approach uses a gap of n nodes between a fast pointer and a slow pointer. By advancing the fast pointer first, both pointers traverse the remaining nodes simultaneously in a single pass, landing the slow pointer right before the node to delete.

derivation.note: The loop runs n + 1 times to establish the offset between the fast and slow pointers.
The while loop runs until the fast pointer reaches the end of the list.
A single pointer update to bypass the target node.

data.time_summary: Line 7 runs n + 1 times and line 10 runs sz - n times. Adding these together yields roughly sz operations total, resulting in O(sz) time complexity.
data.space_summary: Only a few pointer variables are created regardless of the input size, which uses O(1) auxiliary space.
data.takeaway: When you need to find an element at a fixed offset from the end of a singly linked list in one pass, use two pointers separated by that offset.
mistakes: Forgetting to use a dummy node, which causes edge-case failures when deleting the head of the list.
Advancing the fast pointer n times instead of n + 1 times, which leaves the slow pointer pointing at the target node instead of the node before it.

data.overview: The removeNthFromEnd algorithm uses a two-pointer approach with a dummy node to remove the target node in a single pass. By advancing a fast pointer n+1 steps ahead of a slow pointer, the slow pointer lands directly before the node to be deleted when the fast pointer hits the end.
data.intuition: Imagine two runners on a track maintaining a fixed distance of n steps. If the lead runner runs ahead until the finish line, the trailing runner will be perfectly positioned just before the target hurdle to remove it.
